messages.subject: Generalized Linear Mixed Model
messages.subject_clean: Generalized Linear Mixed Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm carrying out an analysis on future time expressions in English on the basis of a corpus of spoken English. I am using a generalized linear mixed effects model (glmer) because when I coded the data I realized that there is considerable variation across conversations concerning the choice of future markers. I have a model consisting of a categorical dependent variable (future time marker WILL or BE GOING TO), a number of independent variables (syntactic, semantic and extralinguistic variables) as fixed effects, and the variable File as a random effect . Not all of my independent variables show a significant effect on the choice of future marker. My questions now are:

1. Is the procedure at arriving at a minimal adequate model the same as for logistic regression models (glm)?
2. How do I find out whether there is reason to assume overdispersion?
3. How do I find out whether my models (both the initial and the final model) have predictive power?
4. How do I determine whether variability within File is stronger than the fixed effects?

I am grateful for any comment on my questions!!
Thanks
Agnes

messages.subject_clean: [StatForLing with R] Generalized Linear Mixed Model
messages.body_plain:
Some brief responses from on the road, I hope others can contribute some more.

> 1. Is the procedure at arriving at a minimal adequate model the same as for logistic regression models (glm)?

There are probably as many opinions out there on that as there are references. I like the procedure outlined in Zuur et al., Ch. 5.

> 2. How do I find out whether there is reason to assume overdispersion?

My thoughts on that are just unvalidated hunches so I prefer not to put them into print. And hope someone else has more definite things to say.

> 3. How do I find out whether my models (both the initial and the final model) have predictive power?

You can compute all the regular things there: classification accuracy, the C-score, and there is now also a proposal out there on how to compute R-squareds for mixed-effects models. I don't have the reference here but google "rsquared.glmm" and you will find it (with code).

> 4. How do I determine whether variability within File is stronger than the fixed effects?

That is probably a quite tricky question because of this issue of bringing the two different types of effects together (fixed vs random). You can get some impression of the variability accounted for by the random effects from the summary output of glmer and the larger the variance, the more the random effect does. (In fact I just completed two papers on multi-level modeling taking at least a bit about that.) It is not clear to me, though, how one can make principled comparisons between fixed and random effects: the latter are not even estimated coefficients of the same type in the model ...

For mixed-effects modeling questions R-lang is probably the more useful list so you may want to try them, too.

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
----------------------------------
Univ. of California, Santa Barbara
http://tinyurl.com/stgries
----------------------------------

About finding out whether fixed effects or random effects is stronger: Actually I want to show that one group of my speakers shows more variability in the use of future time markers than the other. The groups (actually 2 different varieties of English) serve as fixed effects predictors, the individual conversations as random effects. I want to compare the results to a GLM including the same predictors, but without the random effects, and show that only when including random effects the overall variation can be explained. That is why I would also like to know which measure is the best for comparing which of the models predicts the variation more accurately. But I will try a more specialized list for questions like these.

But I have two rather simple things that I encounter difficulties with and maybe someone has a solution:

1. I would like to change the default level in the summary of the model. E.g. it gives me the coefficients for male speakers (female is the intercept) and I would like to get the estimates for female speakers. Does anybody know how to change that?

2. In contrast to the summaries of the lrm() and glm() the summary of glmer() only gives me numbers for the individual predictor levels  instead of the names, e.g. "male" or "female". Is there a way I can change that, maybe add something to the syntax in the call?

Thanks!! Agnes

messages.subject: statistical measure of a "morphology burst" (unequal frequency distribution in a longitudinal learner corpus)
messages.subject_clean: statistical measure of a "morphology burst" (unequal frequency distribution in a longitudinal learner corpus)
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone

I've got a very unequal distribution of the basic verb sapere "know" in my longitudinal corpus of L2 Italian. Until I certain point, a learner uses exclusively the chunk io non so "I do not know". She keeps on overusing this chunk to express other verb forms and meanings for about 4 months. Then from a certain point on, this learner starts inflecting the chunk and morphology appears all in a sudden. My point is that there could be a sort of discontinuity in the acquisition of morphology. My question is: which is the proper statistical tool in R (and relative graph, if possible) to ascertain whether there is a real discontinuity in these distributions?

Thank you so much in advance!!
ciao
Stefano

Hi Stefan,

yes, I am still waiting for the book to arrive :-) In the meanwhile I try to be little more specific with my question.
I have read in various sources that both the Pearson and the deviance residuals should be approximately normally distributed and if this is not the case, a linear model is probably not a good choice. Now a simplistic way to test for normality would be a normality test which, as is well known, will easily generate a significant result due to the amount of data available from even a small corpus. In the literature I found many examples using QQ plots and sometimes histograms for this purpose, but they mostly are from different domains (for exampe using the kyphosis data from rpart: 81 observations on four dimensions - what kind of corpus would that be?) and therefore I am a bit hesitant about interpreting my data as either "good enough" or "too bad".

I know this may seem a naive question, but hopefully this time it is a bit more intelligible. Thanks for your help.

Anne

messages.body_plain: Not a naive question at all but also one that is not easy to answer without writing a chapter ;-) Fox & Weisberg's main point seems to be that one wants to see a constant conditional mean function of the residuals across the range of (a) predictor(s), which seems to be the pretty similar to constant variance of residuals in an lm. However, the same logic as before applies:you also want to make sure that whether apparent violations of normality you find are due to influential data points so I would still recommend looking for those (the car package has many functions that help with that) and throwing in some bootstrapping for good measure.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefan,

thanks for this reply. Well, my residuals are not perfectly normal, they have some tails, however, they are rather weakly populated, so I would conclude my model assumptions are at least not grossly violated. I followed your hint and actually removed some data points using the hats statistic outputted by the influence.measures function and this eased the situation a little bit. I then repeated the modelling and feature selection and this actually gave a model with much better evaluation measures (AIC, cross-validation and the like). Still, the whole process leaves me a bit uneasy. Modelling corpus data in this fashion is not straightforward (neither does it seem straightforward using any other algorithm^^), since this data will always be messy and therefore likely to violate the model assumptions. So what I have now is a somewhat idealised picture based on a balanced data set. I conclude that one should be careful about attributing too much meaning to the coefficients and rather limit oneself to study which of the features were selected (but check for the influence of sampling strategies!) and what their direction is. To get some insight into which of my features are really influential, I took a subsample of my data and predicted probabilities using my model, systematically changing feature values and performing hypothesis tests on the outputted probability vectors. This may still not be the best solution, but it seemed more reasonable to me than to interpret odds ratios and the like.

Thanks for your help.
Anne
